framework.interpretation_is_mine: the DNA triad was named by the project lead and defined nowhere in the repository. This reading is an interpretation, recorded so it can be corrected. Grep confirms zero prior uses of Nous or Aletheia.

delphi.name: Delphi
delphi.gloss: the oracle. What could be built, and what would happen if it were.
delphi.what_it_does: proposes organisms, designs edits, simulates development, scores plausibility
delphi.its_characteristic_failure: fluency. An oracle is never short of an answer, and a design system will produce a cassette for any request put to it - including the two of our three worked requests that are not genome-editing problems at all.

nous.name: Nous
nous.gloss: intellect. What follows from what, independently of whether anyone has looked.
nous.what_it_does: states laws, proves theorems, checks that a conclusion follows from its premises
nous.its_characteristic_failure: vacuity, and its quieter cousin, proving the wrong statement soundly. A theorem with unsatisfiable hypotheses is true and says nothing; a theorem whose English gloss does not match its Lean passes every check this repository has.

aletheia.name: Aletheia
aletheia.gloss: ἀλήθεια - literally UN-concealment, un-forgetting. Truth as disclosure rather than as correspondence.
aletheia.what_it_does: measures against the world, records provenance, refuses, and says what is not known
aletheia.its_characteristic_failure: the false negative that looks like diligence - a check that reports clean because it could not find the field it was checking. This repository produced exactly that twice in one week.
aletheia.why_the_etymology_matters: the Greek word is privative: a-letheia, NOT-hidden, from lethe, forgetting. It is a better name for this layer than "truth" would be, because almost nothing here establishes that a claim is correct. What it does is stop things being concealed - a depicted mesh marked as depicted, a value marked not-established, a scorer measured against data it did not choose. The discipline is not correspondence, it is refusing to forget what a number was made of.

why_three.the_argument: each layer fails in a way the other two cannot see. Delphi cannot tell a good design from a fluent one. Nous cannot tell a sound proof from a relevant one. Aletheia cannot tell you what to build, only what is so. Run any one alone and the characteristic failure goes unnoticed.
why_three.the_worked_instance: the design scorer calls an animal whose dorsal fin begins past the end of its body TYPICAL, and ranks it above 87% of real fish. Delphi could not see it - the score is exactly what the model says. Nous could not see it either, until a registry law was read as a geometric constraint. It took Aletheia, in the form of a search over real specimens, to find an animal the other two layers agreed was ordinary.
why_three.the_asymmetry: the layers are not equal partners. Aletheia is the only one that can say NO on evidence, which is why most of the recent work lives there, and why a refusal is treated as a result rather than a failure to produce one.

goals.name: Agentic biomaterials
goals.note: team members were in the xenobot lab this week
goals.what_it_is: materials that behave: structures made of living cells that move, repair and act, rather than materials that merely have properties.
goals.why_it_sharpens_the_work: a xenobot is the cleanest counterexample to the assumption this pipeline is built on. It is an organism assembled from cells WITHOUT EDITING A GENOME - the design acts on arrangement, adhesion and geometry, and the genome goes along unchanged. Our design surface is an edit list against a reference assembly, which cannot express "take these cells and put them there". The three worked requests already showed one case where the genome was the wrong target; this is a whole class where it is.
goals.what_we_would_have_to_build: a design representation whose primitive is a cell arrangement rather than a sequence edit. .life is closer to this than .organism is - it already carries per-cell position, radius and neighbour-dependent geometry - but nothing in the pipeline can currently propose an arrangement.
goals.the_open_question: what is the unit of agency? A xenobot does things no cell in it does. Whether that is emergence worth a new vocabulary or just mechanics at a larger scale is not settled by watching more of them.

goals.name: Evolutionary biology, and reverse-engineering biological laws and constraints
goals.what_it_is: recovering the constraints that make some organisms possible and others not - and stating them precisely enough to be wrong.
goals.why_it_sharpens_the_work: this is what the 62-law registry IS, and the benchmarks measured how far it reaches. The result is sobering and useful: only 1 of 48 theorem-carrying laws is expressible on the ten body-ratio traits, because the registry speaks in quantities those traits do not carry - two sizes, a population, a power budget, a genotype. A law you cannot evaluate on your data is not yet a constraint on your design.
goals.what_we_would_have_to_build: the missing direction. Everything so far states a law and checks it; nothing INFERS one from data. Reverse-engineering means going from the cloud of real organisms to the boundary of it, and the adversarial search is the first thing here that touches that boundary from the outside.
goals.the_open_question: is a biological "law" a constraint, a regularity, or a habit? Allometric exponents hold until they do not. More measurements sharpen the exponent without telling you whether an exception refutes the law or merely bounds it.

goals.name: Other open biological questions, including origins of life
goals.what_it_is: the questions that are open for reasons other than insufficient effort.
goals.why_it_sharpens_the_work: origins of life is the hardest case of the thing this whole discipline keeps running into: a question where the evidence is gone. Every other item here can in principle be settled by a measurement. That one cannot, because the event left almost no record and the record it left has been overwritten by four billion years of descendants. It is the limiting case of aletheia as UN-forgetting - the thing was not hidden, it was forgotten, and no instrument recovers it.
goals.what_we_would_have_to_build: the honest version is not a simulation of abiogenesis. It is a machine-checkable account of what each proposed route REQUIRES - which is the shape the law registry already has, and the shape the lean-open-problems triage says is worth having: a system that can derive a contradiction from its own accepted premises plus a measurement.
goals.the_open_question: what would count as settling it? A demonstration that life CAN arise a particular way is not a demonstration that it DID. That gap is logical, not empirical, and it will survive any amount of laboratory success.

how_goals_meet_the_triad.the_pattern: each goal is dominated by a different layer, which is some evidence the triad is carving at joints rather than being imposed. Biomaterials is a generation problem, law-recovery an inference problem, and origins an evidence problem.
how_goals_meet_the_triad.the_uncomfortable_implication: the pipeline as built is strongest at the layer the goals need least. Delphi will happily produce a cassette for any request; two of the three worked requests did not need one, and an entire goal - agentic biomaterials - does not involve editing a genome at all.

entries.title: .life — an organism's whole trajectory, in time
entries.why_fun: A file format is the most durable thing you can build. .stl outlived every program that made one, because it was simple enough to be obvious and specific enough to be useful. The idea that a designed organism could have an extension - that you could double-click a creature - is a good enough idea on its own that it is worth seeing whether it survives contact with the biology.
entries.why_science: A .organism describes a design AT REST; stages are metadata. That is the wrong shape for the thing actually being designed, which is a trajectory. And the difference is not cosmetic: A SNAPSHOT CANNOT BE WRONG ABOUT A TRAJECTORY - it has nothing to be wrong with. Make time the primary axis and the file starts making claims that can be FALSE - that this cell count follows that one, that this stiffness falls as that lineage separates - which is what makes them worth storing.

open_questions.q: When is a simulated organism "the same organism" as the design it came from?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: identity over time is a definitional boundary, not a measurement. A trajectory that diverges from its design at stage 4 is either a failed instance of that design or a different design, and no amount of imaging decides which. The file has to pick a convention and say so.

open_questions.q: What is the right granularity for a stage?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: development is continuous and staging is a human imposition on it. Carnegie stages are defined by morphology precisely because age does not work, and the cost is that a stage is a RANGE of days that overlaps its neighbours. Finer imaging gives you more frames, not a principled stage boundary.

open_questions.q: Should a format be able to represent an organism that cannot exist?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: this is a design choice with real consequences either way. Forbid it and you cannot write down a hypothesis; allow it and the file cannot be trusted as a record. .life allows it and requires it to be marked, which is a third answer and not obviously the right one.

Each cell may carry channels: transcriptome (with an in_situ flag), mechanics, geometry, lineage, signalling. And `not_established` is required - a file that lists nothing it does not know is making the strongest possible claim by omission.

An `unknown` carries no value at all - that rule exists because a value of the shape {v: 0.31, unknown: true} slipped past every provenance check in the .organism reader. The census line that falls out is the most useful line in the file: the worked example is 10 measured-secondhand / 5 assumed / 5 depicted / 5 derived / 5 not-established, and NONE measured by us.

blog.title: A File Format That Can Be Wrong
blog.hook: A file describing an organism at rest cannot be wrong about development. It captures one moment and files the others as metadata, and a snapshot has nothing to be wrong with. Turn time into the primary axis and the file starts making claims that can be FALSE - that this cell count follows that one, that this stiffness falls as that lineage separates. Those are the claims worth storing.
body: A .life file is JSON with four required blocks. `identity` says what animal this is. `genome` is an edit list against a named reference assembly, which keeps it in the kilobytes rather than the hundreds of megabytes, and - more importantly - states what the design IS rather than what it resembles. `timeline.stages[]` is the spine. Each stage pins itself with a time, a time unit and a temperature, because development rate is temperature-dependent and a stage time without a temperature is not a stage. The fourth block is the one nobody asks for: `not_established`.

Every value in the file carries a kind and a scope. The kinds are measured, measured-secondhand, borrowed, derived, calibrated, assumed and depicted. What falls out of that is a census, and the census is the most useful line in the file. The worked example - 5 stages, 31 cells, 25 phenotype values - comes to 10 measured-secondhand, 5 assumed, 5 depicted, 5 derived and 5 not-established. Nothing in it was measured by us. Geometry is present on 31 of 31 cells and measured on none. Transcriptome and mechanics are present on 0 of 31.

That last sentence is the point of the format. A file that lists nothing it does not know is making the strongest possible claim by omission, and readers believe omissions. So the absence is a required field. An `unknown` in a .life carries no value at all, and that rule exists because a value shaped like {v: 0.31, unknown: true} sailed past every provenance check in the previous reader. A number with a disclaimer attached is still a number to whatever code reads it next.

Here is where the spec was wrong. It required a field called `elastic_modulus_Pa`, following a published abstract that turned out to be a stale v1 deposit. The authors had since retreated to "relative compliance" - they no longer claimed to have measured a modulus. A field name can impose a unit the measurement does not have, and once a compliance ratio is sitting in a field called `_Pa`, no reader downstream can detect the lie. Requiring pascals does not produce pascals.

The second mistake was worse, because it looked like diligence. The validator stringified its {what, answer} disclosure entries to "[object Object]" and therefore reported the worked example as missing all four required disclosures - while the example answered all four, verbatim, in the file being checked. A false negative in an honesty check is worse than having no check, because the clean report is what gets quoted. There are now 226 tests across the format modules, and the harness injects one fault per assertion and fails any assertion that does not notice. 0 survive.
blog.closing: The convention that remains unsettled is identity. If a simulated trajectory diverges from its design at stage 4, is it a failed instance of that design, or a different design? No amount of imaging decides that, so the format has to pick a convention and say which one it picked. Which is the right one to pick?

entries.title: Benchmarks — the state of the system as measured, not as described
entries.why_fun: There is a particular pleasure in finding out that something you built does not work, before someone else does. It is also the only move in this whole field that is guaranteed to teach you something: a benchmark that confirms what you believed is a wasted afternoon, and one that does not is the best day of the month.
entries.why_science: "61 laws registered, 73 Lean-checked theorems" and "AUC 0.89" are PRODUCTIVITY figures. They measure how much was built and they cannot come out badly. A benchmark has to be able to come out badly, which means the answer has to come from somewhere the system does not control. Three of the four here did come out badly, which is the point.

open_questions.q: Does a plausibility score ever constitute evidence of viability?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: this is a category question, not an empirical one. A Mahalanobis distance measures how unusual a vector is under a fitted distribution. More data makes the distribution better estimated; it does not turn "unusual" into "impossible". We demonstrated the gap - an animal whose dorsal fin starts past its tail scores more typical than 87% of real fish - but the gap is structural and would survive a perfect model.

open_questions.q: What should a benchmark do when the ground truth is itself a model?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: CRISPRscan reaches rho 0.269 on data from the study that fitted it. That is an upper bound, not an estimate, and the only fix is independent data - but "independent" is a judgement about provenance and shared assumptions, not a quantity you can measure.

open_questions.q: Is soundness ever evidence of relevance?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: the Lean layer proves things correctly. Whether the things proved are the things that matter to a design is a question about the choice of formalisation, and no proof assistant has an opinion about it.

blog.title: Four Measurements, Three of Them Bad News
blog.hook: An animal whose dorsal fin begins past the end of its tail scores q = 0.347 on our design plausibility model. That ranks it above 4,068 of 4,673 real fish. The model is not broken. It is doing exactly what it was fitted to do, which is the uncomfortable part.
body: "61 laws registered, 73 machine-checked theorems" is not a result. It is a productivity figure, and productivity figures cannot come out badly - you can only build more or less. A benchmark has to be able to come out badly, and the only way to arrange that is to take the answer from somewhere the system does not control.

Start with the guide score. CRISPR guide RNAs are short sequences that tell the editing enzyme where to cut, and some cut far better than others, so every design pipeline ranks them. Ours ranks them by a score that correlates with measured activity at rho = -0.037, confidence interval [-0.149, 0.073]. The interval includes zero. For comparison we reimplemented CRISPRscan, a published scorer, and derived its position layout by reproducing 25 of its published scores exactly, maximum difference 0.0000 - so the comparison is real and the number is ours to own.

An earlier run of that same comparison gave rho = 0.75, which was thrilling for about an hour. The alignment was off by a fixed offset: reverse-complementing a sequence window flips its flanking regions along with it, so the score was being read against the wrong positions. A good number at the wrong offset is indistinguishable from a good number. It would have shipped.

The design scorer went the same way. Against decoys built by shuffling trait values it reaches AUC 0.891, which sounds like a working discriminator. Against real fish nudged by a quarter of a standard deviation it reaches 0.536, which is approximately a coin. The written prediction before that run said correlation-preserving decoys would score 0.5 "by construction". They scored 0.663, because the fitted Gaussian is overdispersed relative to real fish - the model thinks the space of possible animals is wider than it is. The wrong prediction taught more than the right one would have, which is an argument for writing predictions down.

The proof layer came out clean and still unflattering. All 48 theorem-carrying laws now carry a machine-checked non-vacuity witness, so none of them is true merely because its hypotheses cannot be satisfied. But only 1 of those 48 can be evaluated on the ten body-ratio traits we actually have, because the registry speaks in quantities those traits do not carry: two sizes, a population, a power budget, a genotype. A law you cannot evaluate on your data is not yet a constraint on your design.
blog.closing: None of this tells us whether a plausibility score can ever be evidence of viability. A Mahalanobis distance measures how unusual a vector is under a fitted distribution; more data estimates the distribution better without turning "unusual" into "impossible". The gap is structural and would survive a perfect model, so what exactly would a viability score have to measure instead?

entries.title: The fifth property: a benchmark needs a control
entries.why_fun: Every single control built this week caught MY work rather than the system's. That is a slightly humbling pattern and a very reassuring one: it means the controls are load-bearing rather than decorative, which is not true of most tests.
entries.why_science: A benchmark must take its answer from outside the system, be able to fail, state its scope, and be reproducible. Those four are standard. The fifth is not, and it is the one that actually bit: without a control you cannot distinguish "the system failed" from "my harness cannot tell".

open_questions.q: How do you control a control?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: the regress is real. The Lean control was a weakened mutant that must survive; it came back UNPROVEN, revealing the harness was too weak. But that only worked because I knew independently that the weakened statement was true. At some point a human judgement terminates the chain, and no amount of automation removes that point - it only moves it.

open_questions.q: When a plausible constraint fails on real data, is the constraint wrong or the data?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: one "preanal <= 1 SL" violator is almost certainly a measurement artefact. But overruling a control because the violator looks wrong is exactly the move the control exists to prevent, so it stands. Which way to resolve this is a methodological commitment, not a finding.

blog.title: The Control Keeps Catching Me
blog.hook: Every control built this week caught my own work rather than the system it was pointed at. "The pectoral fin sits behind the head" sounds like anatomy you could teach. It is false for 39% of 4,673 real specimens.
body: Four properties of a benchmark are standard: it takes its answer from outside the system, it can fail, it states its scope, and it reproduces. The fifth is not standard and is the one that actually bit. A benchmark needs a control - something whose answer you already know - because otherwise a clean run is ambiguous between "the system passed" and "the harness cannot see".

The fin constraint shows what that buys. It was proposed as a gate: reject any design whose pectoral fin is in front of the head. Checked against real specimens it rejects 39% of them. So the rule in this repository is now enforced in code rather than in a comment: a constraint may gate only when its recorded support over a real sample is exactly 1.0. The gate that shipped refuses 0 of 4,673 real fish, and that single property is the whole reason it is deployable. A gate that rejects real animals is worse than no gate, because it looks like rigour.

Rejected constraints are not deleted. Each one is kept with the share of real specimens that satisfy it and a `why_not`, so the near-miss stays in the file and the same mistake cannot be made again quietly. One module lost 4 of 8 candidates that way; another lost 7 of 13. The pattern across both is worth stating plainly: a plausible-sounding anatomical rule is about as likely to be wrong as right.

Two of my own mistakes came out of the same week. A mutant in the proof layer was aimed the wrong way - widening a disjunct WEAKENS a conclusion, so the mutant meant to be false stayed true, and the proof assistant said so precisely by placing the attempted counterexample inside the measured band. Separately, I ran a holdout leak gate and a commit in one && chain, so the flagged leak did not block the commit. A gate chained behind the action it guards is not a gate; it is a log line.

The control that worked best was the one designed to succeed. A deliberately weakened mutant that MUST survive came back UNPROVEN, which revealed that the proof harness was too weak to establish even a statement I knew to be true. That diagnosis only worked because I knew it independently.
blog.closing: Which raises the regress the whole scheme sits on: how do you control a control? At some point a human judgement terminates the chain, and automation does not remove that point, it only moves it further back. Where should it sit?

entries.title: Analogy mapping — homology is not function
entries.why_fun: The question "is this the same thing as that?" is the oldest question in comparative biology and it is still not mechanised. Watching agents fan out over twenty genomes to answer it, and then watching most of the answers get thrown out, is the most honest demo this project has.
entries.why_science: DELPHI designs by borrowing a structure from one species into another, which requires deciding when a gene in A is the FUNCTIONAL ANALOGUE of one in B. The pipeline treated orthology as if it answered this. It does not. Homology is shared ancestry; analogy is shared function without it. An ortholog can have diverged entirely, a one-to-many orthologue is not an equivalent of anything, and the convergent cases a design programme most cares about have no orthology at all.

open_questions.q: What makes two structures "the same structure"?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: homology is a claim about history, and history is not directly observable. Sequence, position, development and expression are all correlates, and they disagree - a structure can be positionally homologous and developmentally novel. There is no measurement that returns "same", only measurements that return "similar in this respect".

open_questions.q: How should incommensurable evidence kinds be weighed against each other?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: rescue experiments, synteny, expression similarity and domain architecture are different kinds of evidence, not different amounts of one kind. Collapsing them into a single confidence number requires weights, and the weights are a modelling choice that propagates into every downstream decision. More data makes each kind better measured and does not make them commensurable.

open_questions.q: Is "no orthologue found" ever evidence of absence?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: searching one database is not searching. The strength of a negative depends on the coverage and sensitivity of what was searched, which is a judgement about the search, not a result of it.

blog.title: Same Gene, Different Job
blog.hook: A single mammalian gene can map onto two zebrafish genes, each doing part of the ancestral job. Pick one, call it "the" orthologue, and you get a cassette that fails at the bench for a reason that never appears in the alignment. kcnk5b and its paralog kcnk5a are the live instance in this repository.
body: DELPHI designs by borrowing a structure from one species into another, which means it constantly has to decide whether a gene in A is the functional analogue of a gene in B. The pipeline treated orthology as the answer to that question. Orthology is not the answer to that question. Homology is shared ancestry; analogy is shared function with or without it. An orthologue can have diverged entirely, a one-to-many orthologue is not an equivalent of anything, and the convergent cases a design programme most wants - the same solution evolved twice - have no orthology at all.

The sharpest version is the teleost problem. An ancient whole-genome duplication in the fish lineage left many zebrafish genes as duplicate pairs that have split the ancestral function between them. A mapping that picks one member and labels it the orthologue is not approximately right. It is wrong in a way that shows up only as a failed experiment, months later, with no diagnostic.

So the arithmetic in this module is deliberately unhelpful where the biology is ambiguous. Percent identity has three defensible denominators - alignment columns, shorter sequence, longer sequence - and on one real alignment they give 100.0%, 75.0% and 60.0%. The module returns all three and refuses to pick, because picking is what lets a single number travel downstream as if it were a measurement. The alignment underneath is a real Gotoh affine-gap implementation: BLOSUM62 is verified 24x24 with 0 of 576 entries asymmetric, and a hand-computed case, GATTACA against GATACA, is asserted at exactly 9. The SpCas9 blunt cut is pinned 3 bp to the 5' side of the PAM and asserted six separate ways, because an off-by-one there designs a cassette that integrates in the wrong place.

This entry carries an empty what_went_wrong list, which is not the same as nothing having gone wrong. The error was in the premise rather than in a line of code: the earlier pipeline reported orthology and let the reader infer equivalence. Nothing crashed. Nothing failed a test. The mapping was simply answering a different question from the one being asked, which is the failure mode that no test suite catches, and the reason EVIDENCE_KINDS now keeps rescue experiments, synteny, expression similarity and domain architecture as separate kinds instead of averaging them into a confidence number.

One more refusal worth naming. Every fetch here distinguishes three outcomes that are usually collapsed into one: the API said no, the API failed, and we did not ask. "No orthologue found" in the third case is not evidence of anything, and genome responses are cached outside the repository so that the distinction survives a rerun.
blog.closing: Underneath all of it sits a question measurement does not reach. What makes two structures the same structure? Sequence, position, development and expression are all correlates of homology, and they disagree - a structure can be positionally homologous and developmentally novel. No instrument returns "same", only "similar in this respect". So which respect should a design system believe?

entries.title: Three requests that fail in three different ways
entries.why_fun: A glowing fly, a higher-protein worm, and a cow that burps less. They sound like three versions of the same request and they are not even the same KIND of request, which is the most useful thing about the set.
entries.why_science: Only one of the three is a genome-editing problem in the shape the pipeline assumes. One is not a mapping problem - the function is ADDED, not transferred, and no orthologue exists or is needed. One is polygenic and not a single edit. And one is not about the named organism at all: enteric methane is produced by rumen archaea, and the cow genome encodes no methanogenesis pathway. A system that silently produced a cassette for all three would be wrong three times over.

open_questions.q: Where does an organism end and its microbiome begin?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: the methane case forces this. If the trait of interest is produced by an associated community, is the "designed organism" the cow, the holobiont, or the archaea? Sequencing everything does not answer it - the boundary is a choice about what counts as the unit being engineered.

open_questions.q: What does the person asking for a glowing fly actually want?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: fluorescence needs excitation light, so a GFP fly does NOT glow in the dark; bioluminescence needs a luciferase AND a substrate the fly cannot make. Which one was meant is a fact about the asker, not about the fly, and it changes the entire design.

open_questions.q: Is "heritable" ever the same as "editable"?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: methane yield has non-zero heritability through host effects on the rumen environment. That makes it a selection target. Whether any identified locus is an EDIT target is a different claim, and a heritability estimate - however precise - does not contain it.

blog.title: A Glowing Fly, a Fatter Worm, and a Quieter Cow
blog.hook: Three requests arrive: make a fly glow, raise the protein content of a worm, make a cow burp less methane. They read like three versions of the same job. Only one is a genome-editing problem in the shape the pipeline assumes, and one of them is not about the named animal at all.
body: Take the fly first, because it fails before any biology starts. Fluorescent protein needs excitation light to emit, so a GFP fly glows in exactly 0 dark rooms. Bioluminescence is the other thing people mean, and that needs a luciferase AND a substrate the fly cannot manufacture. Which of the two was wanted is a fact about the person asking, not about the fly, and it changes the entire design. Either way the function is ADDED rather than transferred, so there is no orthologue to find and nothing to map - and the classic tool is transgenesis, not a knock-in.
The worm is a different shape of wrong. Protein content is polygenic. There is no single edit, and a pipeline that returns one has quietly substituted a tractable problem for the one it was given.

The cow is the interesting one. Enteric methane is produced by archaea living in the rumen. The cow genome encodes no methanogenesis pathway, so editing the cow is editing the wrong organism. Methane yield does have non-zero heritability, through host effects on the rumen environment, which makes it a selection target - and a heritability estimate, however precise, does not contain the claim that any particular locus is an EDIT target.

What went wrong here is recorded as an empty list, which is misleading in the usual direction: the system never shipped the error, but only because the three cases were written down before anything was generated. Left alone, Delphi produces a cassette for whatever is put to it - fluency is its characteristic failure - and it would have produced three. So each case now carries the request as the lead phrased it, what is actually being asked, whether the target organism is even the right one, a verdict from a closed vocabulary, and a CRISPR_RELEVANCE field whose job is to say "not this tool". The storyboard has 8 stages per case, and its test asserts both that at least one case refuses before reaching a cassette and that not every case refuses. A demo where everything works is a broken demo; so is one where nothing does.
blog.closing: The methane case leaves a boundary question nobody can sequence their way out of. If the trait you want belongs to an associated microbial community, is the designed organism the cow, the holobiont, or the archaea - and who decides what counts as the unit being engineered?

entries.title: Ecology — the quantity that decides survival is not the one the design optimises
entries.why_fun: The result is genuinely counterintuitive and takes two lines of arithmetic: a design that grows 67% faster still loses. You can show that to anyone in thirty seconds and it changes how they think about what "better" means.
entries.why_science: A design is not released into an empty world. Tilman's R* rule says that with one limiting resource at steady state, the species with the lowest R* = Ks*D/(mu_max - D) competitively EXCLUDES the others - not "does better", excludes. R* turns on affinity at least as much as on rate, and a design optimised for maximum growth rate is not thereby safe. It is often the opposite, because the engineered pathway costs low-substrate performance.

open_questions.q: Is R* the right frame for a release at all?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: R* describes steady state in a well-mixed system. Soil is neither. The honest answer may be that it is the BEST CASE for the design - if it loses here it loses everywhere - but whether that framing is appropriate is a judgement about model applicability, not a measurement.

open_questions.q: If low-substrate affinity decides survival and we optimise rate, is the design objective wrong?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: that is a question for whoever sets the objective. The model can say which quantity decides the outcome; it cannot say which outcome you should want.

blog.title: Faster and Still Dead
blog.hook: Two lines of arithmetic. A design with mu_max 0.5 and Ks 1.0 has R* 0.25. An incumbent with mu_max 0.3 and Ks 0.1 has R* 0.05. The design grows 67% faster and is competitively excluded anyway.
body: Tilman's R* rule is the reason. With a single limiting resource at steady state, the species with the lowest R* - the resource concentration at which its growth exactly balances its loss rate - excludes the others. Not outcompetes on average. Excludes. R* = Ks*D/(mu_max - D), where Ks is the half-saturation constant, so the outcome turns on affinity at low substrate at least as much as on maximum growth rate.

That is awkward for a design pipeline, because maximum growth rate is what a design pipeline optimises and what a growth curve in a rich medium reports. An engineered pathway typically costs low-substrate performance, which means optimising for rate can actively worsen the quantity that decides survival. In the worked example the design would need to be 5x better - in Ks, not in rate - before it won.

Three numbers settle the single-resource question for any organism: mu_max, Ks, and the loss rate D of the environment it enters. So the module refuses to assess any design that lacks a measured mu_max and Ks. It returns the bar the design would have to clear and the three measurements that would settle it, and nothing else. 0 designed organisms in this repository have those measurements, so every assessment currently refuses - which is the honest output, because a competition outcome computed from invented growth constants is indistinguishable from one computed from data.

The two-resource module then corrected the one-resource module, and the correction is on the record even though this entry's what_went_wrong list is empty. A note titled WHAT_R_STAR_IGNORES claimed that adding a second resource makes the single-resource conclusion "lapse entirely". It does not. It GENERALISES: a species with the lower R* on both resources still excludes the other outright, at every supply point. The conclusion lapses only where the two isoclines cross, which is exactly where there is a real trade-off - and overstating the limits of your own result is a way of being wrong that feels like modesty.

The trade-off region has a property worth knowing before anyone releases anything. Reverse only the consumption vectors - who eats more of which resource - and leave all four R* values untouched, and stable coexistence flips to founder control. Same organisms, same affinities, opposite outcome, decided by who arrived first.
blog.closing: All of which assumes R* is the right frame for a release at all. It describes steady state in a well-mixed system, and soil is neither steady nor well mixed. The best defence is that it is the BEST CASE for the design - if it loses here it loses everywhere - but is a best-case model the right thing to hand a regulator?

blog.title: The Clade We Do Not Name
blog.hook: One entire class of animals is unspeakable in this repository. Not the species names, not the class name, not even the id of a claim whose organisms all belong to it. A comparative-biology project with a deliberate hole in it shapes the code in visible ways: one survey keeps all 62 rows of the law registry while naming only 60 of them.
body: The reason is ordinary and strict. A held-out evaluation set is only held out if nothing leaks into the work, and "nothing" includes more than species names. A clade name tells a later reader what the evaluation is about. So does the id of a claim whose organisms are all on the held-out side, even in a file that names no organism at all. A system tuned against a leaked holdout has measured itself, and the measurement cannot be repaired afterwards.

So there is a gate. It scans for the scientific names, the slugs, the database identifiers and the claim ids of the held-out roster, reports leaks and warnings as separate categories, and exits non-zero on a leak. Around it, the code bends. 2 rows in one survey take their law_id from the registry at runtime so the identifiers never appear in source. In another module, 1 of 15 candidate problems was withdrawn rather than written, with a comment explaining why the published count is 14 and not 15.

Two leaks reached a commit anyway. One came from a `git add` on a whole directory, which swept in a half-written module from an agent that was still running. The other came from chaining the leak gate and the commit together with &&, so the gate ran, flagged, and did not block anything. Those are the same root cause wearing two hats: a broad command acting on whatever happens to be there. Both were fixed by redacting the text, never by adding an allowlist entry, because an allowlist entry is a judgement about the scope of the evaluation and that judgement belongs to whoever owns the evaluation.

The gate also has a documented blind spot: it reads 0 .html and .glb files, so those are grepped by hand. Writing the blind spot down is not the same as covering it, and a gate is only as good as the habit around it.
blog.closing: The honest position is uncomfortable. A leak check counts tokens; it cannot count influence. There is no measurement of how much information about an evaluation entered the design that was evaluated, so how much can leak before a holdout stops being one?

entries.title: The scale ladder — organelle to organism, and the two rungs with nothing on them
entries.why_fun: Everyone draws this ladder. Organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organism, five tidy boxes with arrows between them, and the arrows do the work that nobody has done. The fun of building it as a data structure rather than a diagram is that the structure cannot draw an arrow it does not have.
entries.why_science: The gap between levels is not a drawing problem, it is the central unsolved problem of the field. A fin ratio is a number about a FISH; a stiffness is a number about a TISSUE; nothing in this project converts one into the other, and the honest way to say so is to show which rungs carry a representation and which are an identifier with nothing behind it.

open_questions.q: Can a constraint discovered at one level ever be transported to another?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: a packing limit on cells and an aspect-ratio limit on a body are both real, and whether the first ENTAILS the second is a question about the modelling, not about either measurement.

blog.hook: Every talk on multiscale biology opens with the same five boxes: organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organism. The arrows between them do the work nobody has done. We built the ladder as a data structure instead of a drawing, because a data structure cannot draw an arrow it does not have.

So each rung in the file carries three things: its length scale in metres, what in this project actually represents it, and - where nothing does - an empty string rather than an aspiration. Counted that way, 3 of 5 rungs carry any representation and 2 carry none. The organ rung has an identifier and nothing behind it.

The one well-populated rung is the cell, and it is populated from the worked developmental file rather than from a plausible-looking cloud: 31 real cells, all 31 carrying geometry, and 0 of 31 measured. The page says so in those words. A rung populated by a drawing and a rung populated by data must not look the same, or the ladder becomes a picture again.

The payoff is that another result in this project stops being mysterious. Only one of the registry laws that carry a theorem speaks in a quantity our traits carry, and the ladder explains why: the laws are about parts, the traits are about whole animals, and nothing here converts between them. Building the ladder did not fix that. It located it.

entries.title: Mining genomes for functional analogues, and ten pairs that argue with each other
entries.why_fun: The premise of borrowing is that some lineage solved a problem by a route your host does not have. Antifreeze built twice from different ancestors in opposite oceans; an electric organ assembled twice from the same muscle sodium channel; a fish that survives months without oxygen by brewing ethanol in its own muscle. These are the interesting cases precisely because an orthology table has nothing to say about most of them.
entries.why_science: Homology is a claim about ancestry and analogy is a claim about function, and the gap between them is where design pipelines quietly fail. Half of 414 essential yeast genes could NOT be replaced by their human orthologues. So the module does not score orthology: it enumerates seven kinds of evidence that a mapping is functional, keeps them apart, and returns a band of words rather than a number that would be read downstream as a probability.

open_questions.q: When one gene in A corresponds to two in B, what does "the orthologue" even denote?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: nothing. The phrase fails to refer, and picking one of the two is a category error rather than an approximation. More sequencing makes the ambiguity sharper, not smaller.

open_questions.q: Is a convergent solution evidence that the problem has few solutions, or that one route is cheap?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: both predict repeated convergence. Distinguishing them needs a claim about the space of routes that were available and not taken, which is not a thing that leaves a fossil.

blog.title: The Gene That Is Two Genes
blog.hook: A crucian carp survives months without oxygen by brewing ethanol in its own muscle. It does this with a duplicated copy of a housekeeping enzyme subunit that was repurposed for the job. Moving that trick into a zebrafish is exactly the kind of borrow this project exists to evaluate, and it is where the evaluation broke.
body: The pipeline’s assumption is that you can name the host gene that corresponds to the donor gene. Zebrafish has two copies where the question expects one. Ensembl Compara does not even call that one-to-many: it types the relationship as the literal string ortholog_many2many, because the human genes return the same two host genes from either direction.

That is the familiar problem and it is survivable. The unfamiliar one is worse. The donor’s housekeeping copy - the one that kept making acetyl-CoA inside the intact complex - sits in the same clade as the repurposed copy that makes acetaldehyde. So whichever host gene falls in that clade is equally the nominal orthologue of both donor functions. Orthology cannot separate the two things a borrow would have to tell apart, and the ambiguity is not about which host gene to pick but about which job is being moved.

The source paper names neither host gene. It identifies the host copies by clade label, with no symbol and no accession, so even the shape it does report cannot be turned into a mapping. And a symbol search returned a third gene identifier that turned out to be an alternate-haplotype copy of one of the two: counting it would have made a two-gene family look like three.

This is why the module scores evidence rather than orthology. Seven kinds - rescue, loss of function, orthology, synteny, expression domain, domain architecture, positional correspondence - each marked present with what, or absent with why. Across 10 pairs exactly 1 reaches strong, and it is the mouse-into-pig thermogenesis case, where somebody actually performed the substitution and measured the animal afterwards.

The control mattered as much as the result. One pair was included specifically to fail: a fish embryonic arrest against an insect adult arrest, two different things at two different life stages. It banded no-support while its genuine counterpart banded moderate. A scoring system that cannot separate those is measuring enthusiasm.
blog.closing: When one gene in one species corresponds to two in another, the phrase "the orthologue" does not refer to anything. Sequencing more genomes makes that sharper rather than smaller - so what should a design pipeline say when the question it was built to answer turns out not to be open?

entries.title: Lab-in-the-loop candidates, and the five who would be right to say no
entries.why_fun: The nicest thing about reading twenty-four labs’ work closely is how specific everyone’s question is. Nobody studies "fish". They study why a fin stops growing where it does, or how a notochord holds pressure, and the specificity is the thing worth borrowing.
entries.why_science: Lab-in-the-loop only means anything if the loop closes on a measurement someone can actually make. So each profile asks what WE would have to bring, and the answer is often "nothing they need". Writing that down is not modesty; it is the difference between a collaboration proposal and a request for free labour.

open_questions.q: What is the smallest useful unit of exchange between a computational group and a wet lab?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: it is a question about incentives and credit, not about biology. The answer differs per lab and per career stage and no dataset arbitrates it.

blog.title: Reasons They Would Be Right To Say No
blog.hook: Twenty-four labs, read closely enough to quote them accurately. The most useful section in every profile turned out to be the one explaining why that person should probably decline.
body: Lab-in-the-loop is a nice phrase that means very little until you name the measurement someone would actually make. So each of the 24 profiles ends with what we would have to bring, and for several the honest answer is nothing they need. 5 of the 12 fish biologists are in that position by their own published account of what their bottleneck is.

Every quote in the file is verbatim with a source, or it is not in the file. That rule cost more than expected. Two cited identifiers were rejected outright - one resolved to an unrelated paper, one to a paper whose author list did not include the person it was meant to support. Re-reading five web quotes against raw page bytes, rather than a fetch that summarises, caught two more that would otherwise have shipped.

One quote was refused on authorship grounds alone. The best available passage came from a jointly authored essay with per-author sections, and we could not establish who wrote that paragraph. A sentence attributed to the wrong real person is the worst thing a project like this can produce, and there is no version of it that is nearly right.

The privacy rule is enforced rather than promised: the build refuses to write the file if an email address appears anywhere in the serialised bundle. It aborts, it does not warn, because a check that warns and continues is a check that gets ignored. It was also fired against a planted address, so a pattern that silently stopped matching could not pass by matching nothing.
blog.closing: The section about what we bring leads with our own worst numbers rather than our best. That is either the most credible way to start a collaboration or the least persuasive - and which it is stays open until somebody answers.

entries.title: Retro-validation — being wrong nine times out of eleven, on the record
entries.why_fun: There is a particular pleasure in a test you cannot talk your way out of. Four relationships that are already measured, by people who have never heard of this project, sitting in papers from the nineties onward. We write down what we think the answer is, commit it to git, and then look. No wet lab, no approvals, no reagents - just the chance to be publicly wrong by teatime.
entries.why_science: Every other benchmark in this repo was written by the same hands that built the thing being measured, which is the weakest possible footing: a system can look good merely by being well-matched to its own test. A retro-validation borrows an answer key nobody wrote for us. It is a weaker test than a prospective experiment in exactly one way - the answers are findable - and that is what the pre-registration commit is for.

open_questions.q: When a published relationship depends on a modelling convention, whose result is it?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: the myoglobin charge/dive relationship comes out positive at one pH and negative at another, from the same sequences. No further measurement of those species decides which convention is the right one, because the convention is a claim about what the mechanism IS.

open_questions.q: What does it mean to reproduce a result you cannot reproduce the method of?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: the published method models site-specific ionisation constants onto a tertiary structure. We used a uniform model pKa set. The direction agrees at the published pH; whether that counts as a reproduction is a judgement about how much of a method is load-bearing.

open_questions.q: Is a number that no two labs measure the same way a quantity at all?
open_questions.why_data_will_not_settle_it: two labs disagree by 1.35x about the TTX sensitivity of the SAME unmutated channel, which is the size of many of the substitution effects being compared. More measurements of that kind add rows without adding comparability.

what_went_wrong: I MIS-SPECIFIED A PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION FROM THE NAME OF THE QUANTITY. The pre-registration argues at length that myoglobin net SURFACE charge must need structure, and that a sequence-only charge is therefore a weaker proxy. The published methods text says the quantity is the sum over ALL ionisable groups at pH 6.5, not an exposed subset. An agent retrieving the methods section caught it; I had reasoned from the word "surface".

THE MOST STRIKING NUMBER IN THE FIRST TABLE WAS AN ARTEFACT OF MY OWN FETCHING RULE. Preferring reviewed UniProt entries gave one diving mammal more than double everyone else’s charge, because that reviewed entry is a protein-level record with eleven unknown residues. The complete, unreviewed, genome-derived entry puts it mid-pack. Reviewed means curated, not complete.

The charge code could not have caught it. It was caught because a structure predictor refused the sequence and the structure-derived sequence came back short - a check written to catch a wrong accession, catching an ambiguous sequence instead.

A test assertion in the accessibility module claimed two coincident atoms come out fully buried. They do not: whether a sample point counts as occluded is decided by floating-point noise, so the area is arbitrary. The claim was mine, not the code’s, and the module now DETECTS duplicates instead.

The holdout scan in that same test guessed three roster paths, fell back to the largest JSON in the folder, extracted zero taxon names and so scanned for nothing - and passed. It survived its own inverted predicate under --fail-once, which is the only reason it was found.

A correlation was briefly run against minus infinity: rows carry a duration OBJECT whose value may be null, the filter tested the object rather than the value, and Math.log10(null) is -Infinity rather than an error. The statistics module refused it by name, which is why it is a corrected line and not a silent wrong number.

blog.title: Wrong, On The Record, Before Lunch
blog.hook: Every benchmark in this project was written by the same hands that built the thing it measures. That is the weakest possible footing. So we picked four relationships that are already published, wrote down what we expected, committed the predictions to version control, and then looked.
body: The first case is a known relationship between a muscle oxygen-storage protein and how long a diving mammal can hold its breath. The proposal is that like charges keep the protein from clumping at the very high concentrations found in diving muscle, so more charge should mean longer dives. We computed the charge from sequence for 9 species with a sourced maximum dive duration and checked.

The relationship came out positive at one pH and negative at another. Same 9 species, same sequences, same durations: +0.43 at the pH the literature uses, -0.63 at the pH our pre-registration had committed to. That is not noise, and it is not a bug. The entire difference between the two conventions is the histidine count - the correlation between them is 1.000 - and histidine is the one residue that changes its charge across that pH range.

So "net charge" does not name one number. Across these species the two conventions are essentially uncorrelated with each other, which means a pipeline that computes a charge without stating a pH and a set of ionisation constants can produce either sign of a published finding without anything going wrong. Nothing here contradicts the original result: at the original pH we recover the original direction. It says the careful part of their method was the load-bearing part.

The other three cases went against us too, in the opposite direction. We predicted that a rule for predicting the colour an eye pigment absorbs would be good to 8-25 nm; it was good to 4.67 nm. We predicted that toxin-resistance measurements across labs would be too incompatible to assemble six comparable values; there are 18. Being wrong about how bad the literature is turns out to be as common as being wrong about how good our code is.

The most instructive failure was neither. One prediction was mis-specified from the NAME of the quantity: we reasoned at length about a "surface" charge needing structure, and the published methods text defines it as a sum over all ionisable groups with no surface restriction at all. The pre-registration is still in the repository, wrong, because the point of writing it first is that you do not get to edit it afterwards.

And the most eye-catching number in our first draft was an artefact of our own fetching rule. Preferring curated database entries gave one diving mammal double everyone else’s charge, because that curated entry predates genome sequencing and has eleven unknown residues in it. The complete, uncurated entry puts the species back in the middle. Curated does not mean complete.
blog.closing: A relationship that reverses with a modelling convention is still somebody’s result - but whose? No further measurement of those animals decides it, because the convention is a claim about what the mechanism is rather than about what the animals are. That one stays open.

the_four_questions: what stays open regardless of data
how_to_read_this.the_open_questions_rule: an entry under open_questions must be one where MORE MEASUREMENT IS NOT THE KIND OF THING THAT WOULD HELP. "We have not measured it yet" is not an open question in this sense, it is a task. The ones listed are definitional boundaries, modelling choices and category questions - and they are the part of the work most likely to still be interesting in ten years.
how_to_read_this.what_went_wrong_is_not_optional: every entry carries its mistakes. A dev log that records only what worked is a changelog with better typography, and the failures here were more instructive than the successes - a wrong prediction about decoy AUC taught more than a right one would have.

glossary.short: Two genes in different species that descend from a single gene in their common ancestor, separated by speciation rather than duplication.
glossary.long: Orthology is a statement about the branching history of a gene family: the last event separating the two copies was a species split. It is the most-used mapping in this pipeline and the most over-read one. The newcomer error is to treat "orthologue" as "does the same job" - orthology ranks by ancestry and says nothing about current function, and orthology calls themselves differ between methods on identical genomes (Altenhoff 2016), so "the orthologue" is method-dependent before it is anything else.
glossary.concrete_example: analogues/analogy.mjs gives bare sequence-orthology a support band of [0.20, 0.60] for a one-to-one call and [0.05, 0.40] for one-to-many, and refuses an orthology claim that does not state its homology type at all.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Every borrow DELPHI designs rests on a gene-to-gene mapping, and the pipeline upstream of analogy.mjs answered that question with orthology as though orthology were the answer.

glossary.short: Two genes related by a duplication event rather than a speciation, so both can sit inside one genome.
glossary.long: Paralogues arise when a gene is copied within a lineage. The error is to rank them below orthologues for function by default: after a duplication the two copies commonly split the ancestral job, so the copy that inherited the function you care about may be a paralogue of the gene an orthology table nominates. Paralogy is also the first explanation for a knockout with no phenotype, because the sibling copy covers what was removed.
glossary.concrete_example: kcnk5a and kcnk5b are the pair in this repo: crossgraph/README.md records that both map to the single human KCNK5, and the literature attributes the ABSENT kcnk5b loss-of-function phenotype to redundancy between exactly that pair.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: kcnk5b carries the strongest sufficiency claim in the design inventory and the weakest necessity claim, for a reason that is specifically about being one of a pair.

glossary.short: A paralogue pair created by a whole-genome duplication rather than a local one - named after Susumu Ohno.
glossary.long: Ohnologs are the specific case where the duplication was the entire genome, so the two copies started out in corresponding neighbourhoods on different chromosomes. The distinction from a recent tandem or local duplication is not cosmetic, because it changes what you expect of the pair, and the evidence that separates them is conserved synteny rather than sequence similarity. The common mistake is calling any duplicate pair in a teleost an ohnolog pair because teleosts had a genome duplication.
glossary.concrete_example: analogy.mjs records that it is NOT established whether kcnk5a and kcnk5b arose at the teleost-specific whole-genome duplication or by a later local duplication, because no synteny analysis of the pair is held in this repo.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: It is the cleanest case in the repository of a claim that sounds settled, is widely assumed, and has no evidence filed behind it.

glossary.short: Two loci sitting in corresponding genomic neighbourhoods - the same genes, in the same order, around each.
glossary.long: Conserved synteny is the strongest evidence in this project for an ANCESTRY claim: it corroborates that an orthology call is right, and it is the main way to tell an ohnolog pair from a recent local duplication. It is also zero evidence about function, in any degree, and it is the evidence kind most often cited as though that distinction did not exist. Neighbourhood is not job.
glossary.concrete_example: analogy.mjs gives synteny a base band of [0.10, 0.40] and a corroboration weight of 0.5, raised to 0.75 under ALT_BANDS - the sceptic weighting - precisely because it is what distinguishes an ohnolog pair from a local duplication.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: The synteny check that would settle the kcnk5a/kcnk5b origin question is the single missing measurement behind the repo's most load-bearing gene claim.

glossary.short: When one gene in species A corresponds to two or more in species B, so the phrase "the orthologue in B" does not denote anything.
glossary.long: A one-to-many relationship is not an imprecise one-to-one; there is no single object for the phrase to pick out. Picking one of the copies and calling it "the" orthologue is a category error rather than an approximation, and under subfunctionalisation neither copy is the functional equivalent, because neither does the whole job. It shows up at the bench as a partial or absent phenotype that reads as "this gene is not required".
glossary.concrete_example: analogy.mjs refuses to call a one-to-many orthologue a functional equivalent, and gives the honest mapping as a SET: human KCNK5 -> { kcnk5a, kcnk5b }, with the division of labour unknown.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: This is the failure mode of the exact organism the repository designs in, so the refusal is not hypothetical hygiene.

glossary.short: A programmable nuclease system: an RNA guide takes a protein nuclease to a matching DNA site and the protein cuts it.
glossary.long: In this repository CRISPR is a cutting system, not an editing system: it makes a double-strand break, and what happens afterwards is repair, which is where knock-in versus indel is decided. The newcomer error is to treat "we have a good guide" as "we have an edit" - cutting well and mattering are different claims, and in the programme the benchmark was built for, the knockouts are phenotypically normal.
glossary.concrete_example: Two of the three worked design requests in analogues/cases.mjs turn out not to be genome-editing problems at all; the glowing-fly case is a transgenesis problem, and the pipeline produced a cassette for it anyway.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Fluency is named as Delphi's characteristic failure: a design system will emit a cassette for any request put to it.

glossary.short: The RNA-guided nuclease itself; the Streptococcus pyogenes version (SpCas9) makes a blunt cut 3 bp from its PAM.
glossary.long: Cas9 is loaded with a guide RNA, scans for a PAM, checks the adjacent 20 nt against the guide, and cuts both strands. Everything geometric in a cassette layout is measured from that cut, so the enzyme variant is not an implementation detail: a different Cas protein has a different PAM, a different spacer length, and in some cases a staggered rather than blunt break. An off-by-one in the cut position designs an insertion one base off and nothing downstream complains.
glossary.concrete_example: align.mjs cutSite() places the blunt break between the bases at pamIndex-4 and pamIndex-3, i.e. between spacer positions 17 and 18 counting from the PAM-distal end of a 20 nt spacer, labelled basis "mechanistic".
glossary.why_it_matters_here: All cassette coordinates in the repo are relative to that one number, which is why it is stated with its basis rather than inlined.

glossary.short: The short motif immediately 3' of the target site that the nuclease must recognise before it will cut - no PAM, no cut.
glossary.long: For SpCas9 the PAM is NGG, three bases on the same strand as the protospacer and immediately downstream of it. It is a property of the protein, not of the guide, which is why you cannot target an arbitrary position: the available cut sites in a locus are set by where the PAMs are. The error is designing the edit first and looking for a PAM afterwards.
glossary.concrete_example: layoutCassette() refuses with rule `pam_missing` when locus.sequence[pamIndex..pamIndex+2] does not match /^[ACGT]GG$/, on the grounds that the cut site the cassette is positioned against does not exist.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: It is one of the four numbers the cassette module enforces with a stated basis ("definitional") rather than a remembered convention.

glossary.short: The 20 nt of GENOMIC DNA immediately 5' of the PAM: the target itself, not the guide that pairs with it.
glossary.long: Protospacer and spacer are two sides of one pairing: the protospacer is in the genome, the spacer is in the guide RNA. Keeping them separate matters because an oligo as ordered is often not the protospacer - a T7 transcription template carries added 5' G residues that are not genomic, so matching the oligo against a genome fails or matches the wrong place.
glossary.concrete_example: benchmarks/crispr-ontarget queries each guide with its 3'-most 20 nt and then defines the protospacer as the 20 nt immediately 5' of the PAM, which lets an 18-mer and a 22-mer oligo be scored on the same genomic site; 307 of 499 located uniquely in GRCz11.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Without that convention the benchmark would have silently scored 191 unlocated guides as a random sample rather than reporting them as a selection.

glossary.short: The 20 nt variable part of the guide RNA that base-pairs with the protospacer and sets where the cut lands.
glossary.long: The spacer is the only part of the guide you choose, and its length is definitional rather than adjustable: shorten or lengthen it and the cut geometry the whole cassette is positioned against moves by that offset, while the construct still looks correct. Two sequence features reject a spacer outright rather than merely deprioritising it, and one of them is invisible to the eye because the spacer is still a valid 20-mer.
glossary.concrete_example: validateSpacer() hard-rejects any run of 4 or more T (an RNA polymerase III termination signal, so a U6-driven guide is truncated or absent) and only FLAGS a GC fraction outside 40-80 %, because that band is a design-tool convention with no efficiency figure attached.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: It is the repository's cleanest example of separating a mechanistic rule from a convention instead of enforcing both at the same strength.

glossary.short: The chosen 20 nt spacer fused to a constant ~76 nt scaffold that Cas9 binds; the spacer alone is an inert 20-mer.
glossary.long: A single-guide RNA fuses what were originally two RNAs (the crRNA repeat and the tracrRNA) into one molecule. The scaffold is constant, which makes it easy to forget, and that is exactly where a specific failure hides: a truncated or mutated stem-loop stops Cas9 loading, and the symptom - "the guide does not work" - is then chased in the spacer.
glossary.concrete_example: CASSETTE_PARTS.sgrna_scaffold records 76-82 nt with basis "definitional", and SGRNA_PART_ORDER keeps the sgRNA unit (promoter, spacer, scaffold) as a SEPARATE construct from the donor - putting the spacer inside the donor cassette is refused, not laid out.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: It is a recoverable design error the layout engine refuses rather than silently rendering, which is the pattern the whole module follows.

glossary.short: Repair that copies a donor template into a break using flanking sequence identity - the only route that installs a designed insert.
glossary.long: HDR is what turns a cut into an edit: the cell finds sequence matching the regions either side of the break and templates the repair from it. It competes with end-joining and usually loses, which is why arm length, donor form and cell-cycle state all matter. The newcomer error is to expect an efficiency number; this repository asserts none anywhere, and labels every threshold definitional, mechanistic or conventional instead.
glossary.concrete_example: WHAT_THIS_DOES_NOT_PREDICT in align.mjs opens with "HDR efficiency. No number here predicts it", and homologyArmAdvice() returns a BAND (30-60 nt for ssODN, 500-1000 bp for plasmid) with basis "conventional" rather than an optimum.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Refusing to assert an efficiency is the aletheia discipline applied to a module that would look more useful with a fabricated percentage in it.

glossary.short: Repair that rejoins a break directly, without a template, usually leaving a small insertion or deletion at the join.
glossary.long: End-joining is the default outcome of a Cas9 cut and the mechanism behind most knockouts: the indel shifts the reading frame and the protein is lost. It is also what you get when an HDR design fails, which is the trap - the experiment produces edited cells either way, so a knock-in attempt that silently became a knockout still yields sequencing reads and selected clones.
glossary.concrete_example: CASSETTE_PARTS.homology_arm_5 states the consequence of omitting the arm outright: "there is no HDR at all - the donor cannot be templated in, and the cut repairs by NHEJ/MMEJ into indels".
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Every `failure` field in the cassette vocabulary is written to describe the construct that still assembles and still sequences, which is the only kind of error worth a vocabulary.

glossary.short: Donor sequence matching the genome either side of the cut; the strand-invasion substrate that makes repair homology-directed.
glossary.long: Arms are what make a donor a template rather than a loose piece of DNA. Two things go wrong quietly. Too short, and HDR collapses while the surviving events are enriched for one-sided integration - which a single junction PCR scores as correct. Asymmetric, and you get one clean junction and one ragged one, and the usual 5'-junction PCR calls the clone correct.
glossary.concrete_example: CASSETTE_LIMITS enforces a floor of 300 bp per arm for a dsDNA or plasmid donor and 30 nt for an ssODN donor; below it layoutCassette() returns refused with rule `homology_arm_too_short` and the enforced number, basis and source attached, rather than laying out a cassette that cannot work.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: The floor is labelled "conventional" and described as permissive rather than a target, so the number cannot be quoted back as a measured cliff.

glossary.short: A genomic location chosen for an insertion because it supports expression without disrupting anything nearby.
glossary.long: A safe harbour is where you put a construct when the point is to ADD a function rather than alter one. The error is treating it as a free slot: "safe" is a claim about the neighbourhood that has to be supported for the organism and locus in question, and an inserted cassette can still act on transcription next door. Where the goal is addition, the older transgenesis routes are often simpler than a targeted knock-in.
glossary.concrete_example: analogues/cases.mjs treats the glowing-fly request this way: no endogenous fly gene is altered, so germline transgenesis (P-element, or phiC31 at an attP site) is the standard route and CRISPR knock-in at a safe harbour is recorded as possible but not required.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: It is one of the two worked requests that turned out not to be a genome-editing problem, which is the evidence behind the "fluency" criticism of the design layer.

glossary.short: The ordered construct that gets inserted - arms, promoter, coding sequence, tag, terminator, marker - each with its own failure mode.
glossary.long: A cassette is a layout problem as much as a sequence problem, because the parts have an order and the junctions between them are where frame slips and read-through live. The part that is most often omitted is the one whose absence leaves the construct looking complete; the part most often mis-sized is the one whose length is not a multiple of three at a fusion junction.
glossary.concrete_example: DONOR_PART_ORDER is [homology_arm_5, promoter, cds, linker, tag, terminator, selection_marker, homology_arm_3]; layoutCassette() sorts a spec into that order, reports `reordered: true` when it had to, and returns junction sequences with 12 bp of flank on each side for primer design.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: The repo's design layer will produce a cassette for any request put to it, so the vocabulary that says what each part is FOR is also the vocabulary that shows when none of them was needed.

glossary.short: The regulatory sequence that drives transcription of what follows it; which promoter you need depends on what reads it.
glossary.long: A promoter is not a generic "on" part. Two distinct errors appear in the cassette vocabulary: adding one to an in-frame fusion knock-in, where the HOST promoter should drive the insert, gives a second unregulated transcript; and truncating one removes the distal regulatory elements first, so expression survives in the cell line you test and fails in the tissue you care about. For guides there is a third: a polymerase mismatch.
glossary.concrete_example: CASSETTE_PARTS.sgrna_promoter records that a T7 unit delivered as plasmid DNA is not transcribed in the cell and a U6 unit used for in-vitro transcription is not transcribed in the tube - and that U6, being Pol III, also constrains the spacer via the 4+ T termination signal.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: It is the clearest case in the module where choosing the wrong part, not omitting one, is the realistic error.

glossary.short: The sequence that ends transcription and adds the polyA tail; leave it out and transcription runs into the neighbouring genome.
glossary.long: A terminator is the classic omission, because a cassette still looks complete without one. The consequence is read-through: long chimeric transcripts, non-polyadenylated and therefore unstable mRNA, and interference with the next gene along. None of that announces itself as a missing part; it reads as poor expression.
glossary.concrete_example: CASSETTE_PARTS.terminator gives 100-800 bp with the note that common polyA signals (SV40, bGH) sit in the 130-250 bp range, and names read-through as "the classic omission because the cassette still looks complete without it".
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Each part's `failure` field exists so the dev log can say what a missing part does, rather than only that the part is missing.

glossary.short: Adding exogenous DNA to a genome at a site of the method's choosing, rather than editing a chosen endogenous locus.
glossary.long: Transgenesis predates CRISPR and remains the right answer whenever the goal is to ADD a function rather than change one - a reporter, an extra copy, a heterologous protein. The error this project made is the reverse of the usual one: reaching for genome editing because the pipeline is an editing pipeline, when the request did not involve altering any endogenous gene.
glossary.concrete_example: cases.mjs records the P-element route and the phiC31 integrase route (Groth 2004), where fertile injected adults produced transgenic offspring and 100 % of those progeny carried a precise insertion - "transgenesis is simpler, older and better characterised" than a knock-in for a reporter.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Named explicitly as the right deliverable for one of the three worked requests, against a pipeline whose only design surface is an edit list.

glossary.short: Installing a designed sequence at a chosen genomic position, usually by HDR from a donor whose arms match the cut site.
glossary.long: A knock-in is a cut plus a template plus the cell choosing the templated route. Its characteristic silent failure is frame: an insert whose length is not a multiple of three at a fusion junction shifts everything downstream, and the construct still assembles, still sequences, and produces nothing. The check is the junction frame, not the total length - and nothing in this repository translates, so nothing here verifies it.
glossary.concrete_example: CASSETTE_LIMITS.maxInsert caps the sequence between the arms at 5,000 bp as a stated convention - "knock-in protocols are written for inserts of a few kb and switch to other strategies (integrase, recombinase landing pad, serial knock-in) beyond that" - with no efficiency claim for any size.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: Frame verification at a fusion junction is on the explicit list of things the module does NOT predict, which is where a dashboard would otherwise imply it does.

glossary.short: Destroying a gene's function, typically by an end-joining indel that shifts the frame, to ask what the gene was needed for.
glossary.long: A knockout tests necessity, one-sidedly: it shows the gene is required for something, never that it could do another gene's job. The hard part is a knockout with NO phenotype, which is consistent with three different situations that look identical from outside - redundancy with a paralogue, transcriptional adaptation, and the gene genuinely being dispensable - and nothing in the knockout distinguishes them.
glossary.concrete_example: analogy.mjs gives loss-of-function phenotype similarity a band of [0.25, 0.65] and states that an ABSENT phenotype establishes least of all, citing Rossi 2015 and El-Brolosy 2019; kcnk5b is the repo's instance.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: The gene with the strongest sufficiency claim in the design inventory has its necessity evidence missing for exactly this reason.

glossary.short: Putting a candidate gene into a background missing that function and asking whether it returns - the only direct test of function.
glossary.long: Of the seven evidence kinds in analogy.mjs, rescue is the only one that asks the question of interest instead of a correlate of it. It is still not a blank cheque: rescue is directional (B rescuing A does not entail the reverse), assay-specific, and context-specific, and a FAILURE to rescue is weak evidence against analogy because it can fail on codon usage, folding, dose or timing.
glossary.concrete_example: Kachroo 2015 replaced 414 essential yeast genes with their human orthologues one at a time and roughly half could not do the job - which analogy.mjs uses as the base rate for "orthologous means interchangeable" in the most favourable case imaginable.
glossary.why_it_matters_here: It sets the ceiling the whole analogy module is calibrated against: the strongest available evidence kind still earns only a [0.55, 0.90] band.

glossary.short: Degradation of a mutant transcript upregulating a related gene, so the mutant looks healthy for a reason unrelated to redundancy.
glossary.long: Transcriptional adaptation is an active response to the mutant mRNA, not passive backup by a sibling copy.
